_anchors.canvas.w: 64. The widest crater is `crater-c` at 21 units of radius — 44 px across after the lobed rim's crests — and it was 104 when the craters were half the scene wide. He asked for them smaller twice, once for the rocks and once for the craters: a crater wide enough to hold the player is a crater he walks inside rather than past.
_anchors.canvas.h: 48. A crater is a circle seen from about forty degrees, so it is 0.66 as tall as it is wide: the largest is 29 px tall.
_anchors.canvas.originX: canvas.w / 2. Every subject in this project centres horizontally in its cell, so a facing swap or a scale change never slides the body sideways.
_anchors.tones.perMaterial: 5, the Chrono idiom he ranked first on 15/08.
_anchors.frames.walk: 2, the minimum a gait accepts. Nothing in the lunar sky or on its surface moves: the moon is tidally locked, so from a landing site the Earth hangs in one place forever, and a rock is a rock. Two identical frames is the honest way to say 'still' in a vocabulary whose unit is a cycle.
_anchors.light.x: -0.55, the sun, and it is the SAME lamp the astronaut uses. One light source for the whole scene is not a stylistic choice here - it is the fact that there is exactly one on the moon.
_anchors.light.y: -0.5, low. The Apollo photographs were taken with the sun near the horizon, which is when a grey plain reads as terrain.
_anchors.light.z: -0.25, barely on the viewer's side. Held identical to the astronaut: one lamp for the whole scene, because there is exactly one on the moon.
_anchors.light.curve: 1.15, above linear, matching the astronaut. The subjects and the ground have to be lit by one curve or the figure looks pasted onto the plain.
_anchors.outline.enabled: ON, the project's standing answer for holding a shape at small size.
_anchors.outline.inner: on, and it costs almost nothing here because every detail on these bodies is a MARKING - a continent, a cloud, a crater rim. Markings draw no inner line, which is why a globe made of eight parts reads as one sphere.
_anchors.outline.rim: OFF. A line and a rim are two answers to one question, and this project picked the line.
_anchors.outline.material: the ink ramp, a cool near-black.
_anchors.body.scale: 1. Every subject in this project is authored at its true size; nothing is scaled to fake distance.
_anchors.gait.swing: 0.26, held equal to the astronaut so the whole scene shares one amplitude. Nothing here uses it; a gait with no tracks reads no amplitude.
_anchors.texture.speckle: 0. Chrono places every pixel, and noise is the incumbent idiom's signature — the thing the ink verdict of 15/08 most wanted the back of.
_anchors.playback.msPerFrame: 500. Two frames at 500 ms is a one-second cycle that changes nothing, which is the cheapest still this vocabulary can express.
_anchors.playback.scale: 3, the scene's. 3 is the integer scale every micro game blits at; a fractional one would sample pixel art through mud.
_anchors.shadow.steps: 8 px, and it is measured rather than chosen: a sweep at 6, 10, 16 and 24 returns the same shadow area from 6 onward. Past a few pixels the ray has left the body and there is nothing more to block it.
_anchors.shadow.bias: 0.25 px of depth. A convex part cannot cast onto itself - that is settled by identity - so the bias only arbitrates a tie between two DIFFERENT surfaces meeting at nearly the same depth.
_anchors.shadow.strength: 2 ramp steps, DOUBLE every other subject in the project. There is no atmosphere to scatter light into a shadow, so a shadow on the moon goes to nearly black. This is the setting expressed as a number rather than drawn.
_anchors.fill.x: +0.5, opposite the key lamp on the horizontal. A fill placed on the same side as the key lifts the half that is already lit.
_anchors.fill.y: +0.7, from BELOW. This is bounce off the regolith, which on the moon is the ONLY bounce there is.
_anchors.fill.weight: 0.03, the lowest in the project by a factor of five. A fill stands in for sky bounce and there is no sky; what remains is regolith bounce, which is why it is not zero.
_anchors.canvas.originY: 30, canvas.h - 18. A crater's origin is the middle of its bowl, which is where the hole meets the plain; a rock's is the ground under it. Both place by origin rather than by foot, because the ground contact of a depression IS its centre and its lowest painted pixel is its near rim.
